newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF and Pakistan seen close to loan agreement.
newsitem.headline: IMF and Pakistan seen close to loan agreement.

text.p: Pakistan and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) ended talks on Wednesday on a new medium-term loan to Islamabad and appeared close to an accord.

"We have concluded talks with the IMF," Pakistan's Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz told reporters as he emerged smiling after hosting a dinner for an IMF team led by the fund's director for the Middle East, Paul Chabrier.
He declined to comment on the outcome, saying details would be released on Thursday jointly by his ministry and IMF officials, but he added: "Can't you see happy faces around."
Pakistan and IMF have been negotiating for a $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, three-year enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) loan for balance of payments support.
"Talks were frank, friendly and fruitful," Chabrier said before leaving for the evening meeting. "These have proceeded well," he said about the previous talks, but gave no details.
Another IMF official, Antonio Furtado, said "no" when asked if there was any contentious issue to be discussed. "They are meeting because they still have a lot of things to do," he added.
An IMF team started technical discussions with Pakistani officials on July 10 on various aspects of Pakistan's economy and the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) announced in June.
Charbier and his team will prepare the draft of a policy framework paper for consideration by the IMF executive board that will need to give the final approval for any loan.
Aziz has said that the talks will result in a new loan for Pakistan because Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government has already undertaken strucutural reforms ahead of IMF's initial expectations.
Pakistani officials say revenue and spending targets laid out in the 1997/98 budget are generally consistent with the reform programme, but some fine-tuning may be needed.

Pakistan signed a $1.5 billion, three-year ESAF programme with the IMF in February 1994, but the Fund halted disbursements after the former government of then prime minister Benazir Bhutto announced a budget that failed to meet agreed targets.
A balance of payments crisis in October 1995 forced Bhutto to seek an IMF standby loan, which was suspended in March last year, again because of missed targets.
The standby loan was resumed and expanded in December after a caretaker government took over, but the IMF halted it in March when Sharif's government said the targets were out of reach.
But the IMF welcomed Sharif's plans for structural reforms, including tax and tax administration reforms, faster privatisation and a revival of industry and farming.
